tldr: This paper shows that without any cameras or tactile sensors, a humanoid can rely solely on joint encoder tracking errors as a "whole-body tactile channel" to blindly trap a soccer ball, mount a skateboard, and perform complex whole-body manipulation.
hero_caption: Foot-based active soccer ball seeking and trapping, alongside the evolution of the object position estimation error during contact. While subtly wiggling its ankle to search, the moment the foot touches the ball at 0.73 s, the ball position estimation error drops sharply to around 2 cm.
overview:
In recent years, legged robots have mastered "blind locomotion," traversing rough terrain and stairs without cameras. This works because joint encoder histories (proprioception) contain rich information about ground contact and terrain features. Curiously, however, research on whole-body object manipulation (loco-manipulation) still largely takes it for granted that one must add arrays of external cameras, expensive tactile skins, or force-torque (F/T) sensors.

The authors take the opposite stance: how far can a humanoid push dexterous whole-body manipulation using only the built-in joint encoders already found on commercial robots, without adding a single extra sensor? The key lies in the tracking deviation between the "desired joint target" and the "measured joint position" under PD control. When actuators are compliant, tracking errors caused by external forces directly reflect load torques and contact events. In other words, simply feeding previous target commands into the observation vector turns the joint encoders into a coarse, whole-body tactile sensor.

Using Isaac Sim and a physical Unitree G1 humanoid, the authors evaluated four demanding tasks: IMU-free walking, active blind soccer ball trapping, skateboard mounting, and suitcase lifting. The robot learned "active perception"—deliberately tapping and probing its surroundings to induce contact—and demonstrated surprising dexterity. This work convincingly proves that existing encoder signals, combined with purposeful compliant contact, provide a powerful substrate without needing extra hardware.
contributions: Demonstrated on a physical Unitree G1 humanoid that standard joint encoders alone—without cameras, F/T sensors, or tactile sensors—suffice for IMU-free walking, active environmental exploration, and whole-body manipulation.
Clarified the mechanism by which tracking errors (deviation between desired and measured positions) in compliant PD control act as a whole-body tactile signal that elicits active probing motions.
Trained a diagnostic state estimator on proprioceptive histories alongside the policy, quantifying the sharp drop in object pose estimation error precisely at the moment of informative contact.
Showed why distilling from a privileged teacher fails in partially observed exploration settings, highlighting the necessity of reinforcement learning from scratch.

sections.heading: Why can a humanoid manipulate objects blindly without "eyes"?
sections.summary: Starting from a simple question—why not use proprioception-only control in manipulation just as we do in locomotion?—this work examines how far whole-body manipulation can go using joint tracking errors as tactile feedback, stripped of all extra sensors.
sections.details:
In humanoid locomotion, "blind walking" without cameras or LiDAR is already a standard approach. By observing joint encoder and IMU histories, robots infer contact states on stairs or uneven ground and maintain robust gaits. However, turning to manipulation, the prevailing trend is still to mount cameras all over the body or attach expensive tactile skins and force-torque sensors. The authors found this disparity striking: if locomotion captures such rich information from onboard sensors alone, can manipulation do the same?

To answer this question decisively, this study intentionally discards all cameras, markers, and external sensors on a Unitree G1 humanoid. Four tasks were evaluated: (1) robust bipedal walking without even an IMU, (2) actively seeking and trapping a soccer ball with a foot, (3) mounting a randomly placed skateboard, and (4) locating and lifting an easily toppled suitcase by its handle.

The core insight is a standard trick in legged robot RL: including the previously commanded joint targets in the policy observation. Under compliant PD control, the difference between desired and measured positions (tracking residual) directly reflects external load torques. As the robot actively reaches out to touch its environment, the encoder signals themselves serve as an active, whole-body tactile channel.

sections.heading: Bridging adaptive locomotion and "active touch"
sections.summary: This section reviews prior work in proprioceptive adaptive locomotion (such as RMA) and interactive perception through contact. The study uniquely reframes compliant control itself as a whole-body tactile sensor without relying on specialized tactile devices.
sections.details:
Two major research threads form the backbone of this work.

The first is proprioceptive adaptation. In legged robotics, frameworks like RMA infer latent environmental parameters—such as friction or step heights—directly from joint histories. Recent work like SoftMimic and GentleHumanoid integrates impedance control principles into reinforcement learning to achieve safe, gentle physical interactions, such as hugging humans. However, those methods use compliance primarily for safety and stability. This paper goes a step further: it treats the deviations caused by compliance as sensory inputs to perceive the external world.

The second is active touch and interactive perception. A robot cannot learn much about an object simply by resting against it statically. Purposeful interaction sequences—tapping, stroking, pushing—are required to uncover contours, stiffness, and mass. While prior work has predominantly relied on ultra-high-resolution sensors like GelSight, this paper asks: can we achieve similar interactive perception across the entire body using coarse joint tracking errors?

sections.heading: Formulating the vision-free humanoid control problem
sections.summary: Using a Unitree G1 controlled via a position PD interface, the task is formulated as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) where true object poses cannot be observed directly.
sections.details:
The experimental platform is the commercial Unitree G1 humanoid robot with whole-body actuators. Sensory inputs consist only of joint positions $q_t$ and velocities $\dot{q}_t$ from joint encoders, plus the onboard IMU (projected gravity vector and base angular velocities). In certain experiments, the authors even exclude the IMU to test an "encoder-only" configuration.

The robot is commanded at 50 Hz via a PD position control interface outputting desired joint targets $q^{\text{des}}_t$. Rather than using high gains to make actuators stiff, moderate compliance is maintained.

### III-A Problem Statement
Under this setup, the problem is formulated as a POMDP. The agent (policy $\pi_\theta$) has access to neither external camera feeds nor ground-truth object states; it observes only short sensory histories and its own past actions. Under these tight constraints, the authors pose two core questions:
- Can whole-body manipulation tasks involving large spatial uncertainty be solved using only proprioception and compliant control?
- How well can critical task variables, such as object pose, be decoded from short proprioceptive histories following physical contact?

sections.heading: Tracking errors become touch: learning and estimation mechanisms
sections.summary: Policies are trained with PPO in Isaac Sim using simple MLPs that take just 0.1 s (5 steps) of history. A separate, decoupled state estimator is trained concurrently to quantify how much object information is unlocked by contact.
sections.details:
### IV-A Reinforcement Learning Formulation
Policies were trained using GPU-parallelized Isaac Sim and PPO from RSL-RL. The policy network is a simple MLP with hidden layers $[1024, 512, 256]$. For object manipulation tasks, it takes an observation history $h_t$ spanning the past $K=5$ steps (just $0.1\,\mathrm{s}$ at $50\,\mathrm{Hz}$ control).

The key mechanism is the implicit contact signal. Policy observations include not only current joint positions $q_t$, but also the previous targets $a^q_{t-1}$. Because PD torque is determined by $\tau_t^{\mathrm{PD}} \approx K_p (q^{\text{des}}_{t-1} - q_t) - K_d \dot{q}_t$, tracking errors $e_t$ map directly to external torques. Thus, without explicit torque sensors, observing error trajectories over time lets the policy know when it has hit something and which way resistance is pushing.

Training uses an asymmetric Actor-Critic setup: the critic receives privileged simulator state (e.g., ground-truth object poses and velocities), while the actor receives none. Domain randomization over link masses, friction coefficients, and motor strengths bridges the sim-to-real gap.

### IV-B Variable Stiffness Control
For the delicate suitcase task, variable stiffness control (+VS) is introduced. In addition to target positions, the policy outputs scaling factors $\alpha_t \in (0, 1)$ that reduce PD gains per joint. This allows the robot to remain compliant and soft while searching, then stiffen up once it lifts the object.

### IV-C Proprioceptive State Estimation
To visualize and analyze how well the robot understands the environment through contact, the authors train an auxiliary state estimator $\phi(h_t)$. This separate MLP takes the same observation history and predicts the 3D position and orientation of the object. Crucially, **no gradients from this estimator flow into the policy**. It serves purely as a diagnostic probe to measure how much task-relevant state becomes decodable as a byproduct of active contact.

sections.heading: Four challenging tasks: from blind trapping to skateboarding
sections.summary: Evaluations span IMU-free walking, soccer ball trapping, skateboard mounting, and suitcase lifting. While student policies distilled from privileged teachers fail due to a lack of exploratory drive, RL policies trained from scratch discover active perception: probing and pinpointing objects upon contact.
sections.details:
Four tasks systematically test the strengths and limits of this approach.

### V-A IMU-Free Walking and Push Recovery
First, a locomotion test: the IMU is removed entirely to see if joint encoders alone support walking and disturbance recovery. The policy with encoder and previous action history (-IMU+PE) stays upright when pushed by external forces (Fig. F1). The robot infers tilt and external forces purely from joint deflections caused by foot-ground collisions. In contrast, removing past action observations (-IMU-PE) causes both state estimation and posture recovery to collapse.

### V-B Active Football Localization and Trapping
Here, a soccer ball is placed randomly within a $0.3\,\mathrm{m} \times 0.4\,\mathrm{m}$ area in front of the robot, which must find and trap it with its right foot (Fig. F2).
A comparative result stands out: student policies distilled from a privileged teacher that sees the ball achieve very low success rates; they learn only lazy motions, planting the foot near the center of the distribution. Imitation learning cannot easily reproduce the exploratory phase before contact. In contrast, blind policies trained with RL from scratch learn an active search behavior, lifting the foot and wiggling the ankle to scan the floor. As shown in Fig. F3, the instant the foot taps the ball (at 0.73 s), the state estimator's error plummets to ~2 cm, and the foot promptly secures the ball.

### V-C Blind Skateboard Mounting
Mounting a rolling skateboard is a dynamic task difficult even for humans. The board is initialized with position variations and orientations within $\pm 22.5^\circ$. As shown in Fig. F4, the robot taps the nose or tail with one foot to confirm location or drags the board closer before committing to a confident, two-footed mount.

### V-D Gentle Blind Manipulation (Suitcase)
This task requires finding the recessed handle of a thin suitcase on a table and lifting it without knocking it over. Excessive contact force easily tips the suitcase. With variable stiffness control (+VS), the policy keeps its arm compliant, sliding gently along the table and suitcase surface before stiffening to lift the handle cleanly (Fig. F5). Constant stiffness policies tend to tap aggressively and frequently tip the suitcase, whereas variable stiffness dramatically cuts tipping rates.

sections.heading: Key takeaways and limitations: can this replace tactile skins?
sections.summary: The paper outlines three common insights (the failure of distillation, the unimportance of estimator feedback, and contact-driven decoding) while discussing limitations such as coarse spatial resolution and sim-to-real sensitivity.
sections.details:
Across all experiments, three consistent findings emerge:
- **Limits of Teacher-Student Distillation**: In partially observed tasks where exploration is essential, distilling privileged teachers causes policies to settle into lazy local minima targeting the center of the prior distribution. Active probing behaviors only emerged through RL from scratch.
- **Estimator Feedback is Unnecessary**: An ablation feeding predicted object states back into the policy (+SE) showed no gain over raw proprioceptive histories; in fact, early noisy estimates can degrade exploration.
- **Information Unlocked by Contact**: Active contact enables remarkably accurate decoding of object pose and size from just 0.1 s of joint history.

Nevertheless, clear limitations remain. The primary constraint is coarse spatial resolution. Because tracking errors are aggregate joint-level signals, localizing precise contact locations along a link is difficult, and simultaneous multi-point contacts create ambiguity. The approach is also sensitive to sim-to-real discrepancies in actuator compliance and friction. Furthermore, relying on fixed-window (5-step) MLPs prevents long-term evidence accumulation, which will require memory architectures like RNNs or Transformers to retain contact histories over several seconds.

sections.heading: Conclusion: joint encoders are a dormant whole-body tactile sensor
sections.summary: Compliant actuation paired with joint encoders provides a potent baseline for whole-body manipulation without extra hardware. The authors conclude that richer modalities like vision and high-density tactile sensors should be layered on top of this proprioceptive bedrock.
sections.details:
This study demonstrates that standard joint encoders and PD tracking errors on commercial humanoid robots can serve as a practical, whole-body active tactile sensor. By generating purposeful contact motions, the robot extracts necessary environmental cues to walk, trap balls, mount skateboards, and handle suitcases entirely through touch.

The authors do not argue that vision or tactile skins are obsolete. Rather, they advocate a design philosophy: establishing this resilient proprioceptive baseline ensures that robots remain capable even under camera occlusion or darkness, creating a firmer foundation onto which multimodal perception can be layered.

takeaways: Tracking errors in compliant joint PD control act as an effective whole-body contact signal without requiring extra sensors.
In partially observed exploration tasks, RL from scratch outperforms teacher-student distillation, which often falls into lazy, non-exploratory local minima.
Object pose estimation error plummets the moment physical contact occurs, demonstrating that purposeful contact motions function directly as perception.
Thoroughly exploiting onboard proprioception creates a robust foundation before layering on costly tactile skins or computer vision.
limitations: Spatial resolution is inherently low because tracking errors reflect joint-level torque, making it difficult to pinpoint exact contact locations along a link.
Performance depends on accurate modeling of actuator compliance and friction; sim-to-real gaps in PD dynamics can degrade transfer.
Short MLP history windows (5 steps / 0.1 s) cannot retain contact memories over several seconds, preventing long-horizon logical exploration.
